Key takeaways

  1. Your first social media hire is almost always a generalist social media manager. From there, layer in specialists (paid, content, community, analytics) based on your most pressing goals, not trendy titles.
  2. Know when it’s time to hire. If your DMs are overflowing, engagement is flat, or your one-person team is burning out, that’s your sign to bring in backup. Growth on social means growth on your team, too.
  3. Pay transparency speeds up hiring. Social media manager salaries in the US average roughly $91,000 per year in total pay, according to Glassdoor’s data, with wide variation by experience, location, and company size.
  4. Write job descriptions that are specific. Separate must-have skills from nice-to-haves, name the platforms the role requires, and be real about day-to-day tasks.

What does a social media team look like in 2026?

In 2026, a social media team blends human creativity and strategic thinking with AI-powered efficiency. That might look like one full-time social media manager leaning on AI to grow a startup, or a dozen people across an enterprise team, each with complementary specialty skills.

So who’s actually on a social media team? It depends on three things:

  • Organization size: A complex, multinational, multi-brand organization will need a larger, more diverse team than a local business that operates one shop from one location.
  • Goals: Ambitious, wide-ranging growth needs more hands and a broader range of skills.
  • Channels: The more platforms you’re on, the more people and skills you’ll need. For example, to build brand awareness on LinkedIn, you might need just one person with the right skillset. To reach a multi-generational audience with organic and paid strategies on Facebook, TikTok, and X, you’ll need more people with a wider skillset.

Your social media team rarely works in a vacuum. Their goals and tactics often overlap with content marketing, customer care, growth marketers, and the brand team.

One ‘social media’ hire frequently covers tasks spanning several disciplines.

Key takeaways

  4. Targeting options include demographics, interests, behaviors, custom audiences, lookalike audiences, and Meta’s AI-powered Advantage+ audience for lower costs.

What is Facebook advertising?

Facebook advertising is the practice of running paid promotions across Meta’s family of apps, including Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and the Audience Network, to reach specific audiences with text, image, and video creative. It gives businesses a way to put their message in front of the right people at scale, with precise targeting and measurable results.

Meta’s ad audience is one of the largest in digital marketing. Meta’s own reporting shows an average of 3.48 billion daily active people across its apps in June 2025, which gives advertisers an unmatched pool of potential customers.

Facebook ads run through an auction system. When you set up a campaign, you tell Meta your objective, audience, and budget. Meta then decides which ads to show each person based on a mix of your bid, the estimated action rate, and ad quality. You don’t pay more than you need to win the auction, and Facebook’s algorithm works to deliver your ad to the people most likely to act on it.

What has changed most over the past two years is how much of that work Meta’s AI now handles. With 98.7% of Meta’s app revenue coming from advertising, the company has invested heavily in Advantage+ campaigns, automated audience discovery, and AI creative tools that shift the advertiser’s job away from manual setup and toward feeding the system good creative, clean conversion data, and clear goals.

In short, Facebook advertising combines massive reach with granular control, making it a core channel in any paid social strategy.

What affects your Facebook ad costs?

Several factors influence what you’ll pay to run Facebook ads. Understanding them helps you control spend and improve efficiency.

  • Ad quality and relevance: Higher-quality, more relevant ads win auctions at lower costs.
  • Placement: Some placements, like Feeds, tend to cost more than others, like Audience Network.
  • Time of year: Costs spike during high-demand periods like the holiday shopping season.
  • Industry: Competitive industries such as finance and insurance typically see higher costs per click.

How much does 1,000 views cost on Facebook ads?

A thousand views on Facebook, measured as cost per 1,000 impressions (CPM), typically costs between $5 and $18 depending on your campaign objective. Awareness campaigns sit at the low end of that range, while sales and lead campaigns sit at the high end because they compete for higher-intent audiences.

CPM also shifts based on placement, audience competition, and creative quality. Feed placements usually cost more than Audience Network, and seasonal demand can push CPMs well above these benchmarks during peak retail periods. If your CPM climbs sharply without a matching lift in results, refreshing creative is usually the fastest lever to pull.

Is $5 or $10 a day enough for Facebook ads?

Yes, $5 or $10 a day is enough to run Facebook ads, but what you get from that budget depends on your goals. articles.title: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance. They also share that attempts to control crawler traffic can sometimes accidentally block Googlebot and harm Search visibility.

Moving To A CDN Can Cause Googlebot To Increase Crawling

Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests. Google’s automated crawling systems interpret the improved performance as an indication that more crawling is possible and responds by gradually increasing the crawl rate.

CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.

When Google increases the crawl rate, the initial crawl is handled by the origin server. But now Googlebot is hitting the server more aggressively and it’s this that can overwhelm the origin server, initially.

“For one, suddenly the crawling metrics suggests the site can handle a larger amount of crawling. And on the flip side, because the CDN caches aren’t yet populated, the origin server still has to serve the requested pages.

Basically, CDNs take the valve off the hose, so now crawlers are drinking from a fire hose.”

“Under normal circumstances, our crawlers operate under an important rule. When a server responds faster, the crawlers assume the infrastructure is healthy and slowly ramp up crawl speed.

…So the crawlers see how fast the server responds, get really excited, and start to crawl the entire site at a higher, higher, and higher speed. But it’s a trap.

People assume a CDN can catch a crawl spike from day one, but …The cache has to be filled up with the assets off the site first.”

Gary Illyes explained that on a first request for a page the CDN has to fetch the page from the origin server first to populate the cache with the content. It’s not until the second request for the page that the cache is populated with the content and begins doing its job.

“…which means your origin server may get slammed by the flood anyway. Now, to be fair, our crawlers take time to ramp up. It won’t happen in a millisecond.

An empty cache means your origin server is still doing all the heavy lifting. Until that cache is populated, your CDN isn’t acting as a shield just yet.”

A CDN cannot serve an un-cached URL without retrieving it first from the origin server and that only happens after a request for that URL is first made. Crawlers visit large numbers of URLs virtually all the time and can generate a substantial amount of origin traffic before the CDN’s caches are fully populated.

CDN Bot Protection And Accidental Googlebot Blocking

This next issue involves accidentally blocking Googlebot and triggering a reduced search presence because Google can no longer crawl and index URLs from a website. Illyes and Prommawin explain it in the context of a website admin flipping a switch at Cloudflare and inadvertently blocking Googlebot.

This is a real problem, I recall an instance in which a popular website’s massive traffic dried up whenever Cloudflare was activated and would return once they turned it off. They had a devil of a time diagnosing why this was happening and the customer service people at the time were unable to help them. It may have been the case, as Illyes and Prommawin noted, that the admin had turned on a strict bot filter that inadvertently blocked Googlebot.

Illyes offered an example of an admin doing exactly that:

“They look at the spiking traffic, assume they are being aggressively scraped by botnets, and naturally, they panic.”

And what sometimes happens next is that an admin might turn on “blanket security rules” that block Googlebot.

“In panic, one might log into their CDN dashboard and turn on the setting to block bots entirely.

…If the CDN detects automated requests, it intercepts them with a CAPTCHA challenge, asking them to click pictures of traffic lights to prove they’re human.

…It sees automated requests, flags it as a bot, and then intercepts with a CAPTCHA. And since our crawlers cannot identify a traffic light, they fail the test.”

What eventually happens with prolonged Googlebot blocking is that Google will begin dropping the pages from the index.

Prommawin suggested that site admins should configure their CDN to allow known and trusted crawlers. This is a method called whitelisting where only crawlers that are on the “allowed” list can get it and all other crawlers cannot.

They also recommend the use of CDN-level rate limiting of Googlebot if the requests on the origin server lead to downtime which can negatively impact legitimate human traffic to the website.

When a site initially starts out with a CDN, the CDN does not have a cache of a website’s content. The cache doesn’t get loaded until it’s requested by a browser or crawler visit.

Cache pre-warming is the process of requesting content from a site so that the content gets loaded onto the CDN. This ensures that the content is already loaded onto the CDN before users request it, which ensures that the content is delivered quickly without the CDN having to first retrieve it from the origin server (the server where the actual content files exist).

Illyes recommends “pre-warming” the cache by programmatically requesting URLs from it so that thE cache is populated in a controlled manner.

“And to survive augmenting your site with a CDN, see if you can pre-warm the caches by programmatically fetching your top URLs through the CDN before you open the floodgates to search engines.”

articles.title: The New Competitive Edge in AI-Powered Advertising
articles.fullContent:
By Ashley Cisneros Mejia This post was created in partnership with Atlas Cloud

An ad that once required weeks of production and a six-figure budget can now take only a couple of days and a few thousand dollars to create. As AI lowers the barriers to producing creative, brands now have to decide how to use the newfound capacity to make advertising that consumers actually want to see.

At the ADWEEK House Commerce Summit, a panel co-hosted by Atlas Cloud examined the implications for creative strategy, agency relationships, and the future of personalized advertising.

Kicking off the discussion, Matthew Spradlin, VP of new business development at Atlas Cloud, illustrated the cost difference with an ad he produced over a couple of days using AI tools. Including post-production, he estimated the expense at roughly $3,000. A traditional production of similar scope could run into hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The savings are striking. The possibilities they create are considerably more interesting.

With production costs falling, brands can experiment with variations that once would have been impractical. Yet more volume brings its own challenge: understanding which messages will resonate with whom.

Colin Mo, head of product marketing at Atlas Cloud, captured the ambition as creating “tailored, bespoke experiences for each individual.”

For Kai Tier, executive director of creative technology and AI at Barbarian, a creative and innovation agency, the priority is making that level of personalization practical across the consumer journey.

“You’re producing maybe 100,000 versions of the ad, but the user should only see the four that make sense for them along the purchase funnel,” Tier explained.

AI-powered production tools are making it easier to adapt existing creative for different audiences and markets. Spradlin described customizing an animated Adidas advertisement for international markets, with versions in seven languages. “We did that in a day,” he shared.

Another opportunity lies in how brands allocate their budgets. Money once consumed by the basics of creative production can now support more ambitious work, including intelligent systems that tailor brand interactions to individual consumers.

Integrating AI into established business operations draws on a wider range of agency expertise.

Agencies are now helping clients manage the risks of adopting new technologies, particularly when existing governance processes and brand protections need to carry over into automated workflows.

These responsibilities have pulled creative teams into closer collaboration with legal counsel. Tier described working with clients to evaluate AI models, assess generated content, and maintain the internal safeguards that protect their companies. Establishing those protections, he suggested, gives brands greater confidence to pursue ambitious creative ideas.

Consumer expectations will also shape how far brands can take personalization. Tier expects AI agents to give people greater control over their purchasing journeys, potentially challenging brands’ access to customer data.

Maintaining consumer trust requires “being transparent with the user about what the value exchange is and making sure that they’re bought in,” he added.

articles.title: Why Brands Need to Rethink the Business of Creator Commerce
articles.fullContent:
By Ashley Cisneros Mejia This post was created in partnership with Button

Creators are becoming sophisticated commercial partners, with capabilities and financial interests that extend well beyond content delivery. Their relationships with brands are evolving alongside their companies.

During an ADWEEK House Commerce Summit panel co-hosted with Button, industry leaders and creators examined the changing economics of influence, from the investments behind content production to the challenge of measuring sales.

Creator commerce has grown increasingly complex, with creators taking a more active role in how their content generates revenue.

“They are entrepreneurs. They are not influencers. They are buying ads for their own content so that they can make more money,” said Mike Jaconi, co-founder and CEO of Button.

Some creators manage their own advertising operations, with in-house teams overseeing media buying and performance. Others hire agencies for that expertise, adding another layer of business management to their work as content producers.

The creative work has grown more ambitious, too. Sarah Randall, a content creator who produces a lifestyle and home renovation series with her husband, predicts a shift toward episodic storytelling, with brands integrated into ongoing narratives rather than one-off sponsored posts.

Such productions require intense coordination. Randall described shoots involving professional cameras, lighting, childcare arrangements, and months of preparation. When agencies restrict direct access to brand decision-makers, delayed approvals can disrupt an entire production.

“We just want to talk to you, the brands. We want to create a good story together,” Randall stressed.

The commercial value of creator content isn’t always reflected in its popularity. Ali Thomas, co-founder of The Bargain Sisters, recalled joking about posts that attracted only a few thousand views yet generated substantial affiliate earnings.

“We’ll be able to put our kids through college based on what we earn off of that,” she shared.

Other posts could also go viral without producing meaningful sales. But as Randall noted, engagement remains valuable for brand awareness campaigns. Success depends on the partnership’s objectives.

Jaconi warned that faulty commerce infrastructure can further obscure results.

“I wish that they—the marketers, the retailers—would consider how much revenue they’re losing by having bad links, faulty attribution, and really inconsistent shopper experiences,” he pointed out.

For Cassie Thomas, co-founder of The Bargain Sisters, that risk influences which retailers receive the Sisters’ promotion. “We just won’t link unless we have deep linking. We just won’t,” she said.

Randall illustrated the problem: When an affiliate link opens a retailer’s app without preserving tracking information, the creator can lose commission while the retailer loses visibility into the referral.

Jason Fairchild, CEO of tvScientific by Pinterest and general manager of programmatic and affiliate at Pinterest, sees an opportunity for more comprehensive measurement. Pinterest connects consumer intent with visually compelling creator content. Fairchild advocates combining view- and click-based data to assess incremental impact.

“For me, it’s the full impact of a given ad, meaning not just the last click,” he explained.

Looking toward 2027, Jaconi expects creator content to power larger media investments, where “creators will create this organic content, and then that content will be converted into giant paid media campaigns.”

articles.title: What Verified Purchase Data Unlocks for Streaming Advertisers
articles.fullContent:
By Mindy Charski This post was created in partnership with Magnite

Connecting the dots between an ad exposure and a sale has rarely been easy. Today’s fragmented buying behavior and growing number of shopping touchpoints, including CTV, are adding to the challenge.

During an ADWEEK House Commerce Summit fireside chat co-hosted with Magnite, Sabir Muhammad, lead, brand partnerships at Magnite, sat down with Jim Prandato, global head of ads partnerships at PayPal Ads, to discuss how PayPal is helping brands close the measurement loop, providing other valuable insights, and thinking about shoppable storefronts .

Using transaction data to boost CTV campaign performance

Prandato began the conversation with a bold statement: “Connecting CTV, or the biggest screen in the house, with actual true product purchase data through closed-loop measurement is the greatest untapped opportunity in our industry.”

He subsequently outlined how PayPal, which also operates Venmo and PayPal Honey, is helping advertisers capitalize on that opportunity with purchase data it gathers across millions of merchants.

The workflow PayPal enables starts with pre-campaign insights: Brands can analyze product purchases to understand consumer behavior, which can inform messaging. For example, it’s helpful to know transactions relating to pickleball have significantly tapered off—running creative about the sport could make an ad look passé, Prandato warned. Next, brands can build unique audience segments, activate campaigns, and access closed-loop measurement based on financial-grade data.

Muhammad shared that he and his team partner with PayPal to support advertisers that are activating programmatically.

“Brands are really leaning into the PayPal data because you can find verified data that is scaled in areas where traditionally it’s been really hard—business-to-business being one of those areas,” he said. For instance, now that many people use Venmo to pay for their haircuts, Magnite can leverage Venmo data to help advertisers find hairdressers.

That example prompted Prandato to highlight that Venmo is increasingly becoming more of a point-of-sale tool, not just a peer-to-peer payment option. “There are really unique audiences that we can build off of that,” he noted, including emoji-based targeting.

When the conversation shifted to shoppable storefronts on streaming services, Prandato said PayPal thinks it can have a big impact in the space because it owns the payment rails and consumers are familiar with the company.

PayPal has already rolled out storefront ads on the open web for display and online video that enable consumers to purchase within the ad, he explained. The next opportunity will come from figuring out the right consumer experience for CTV.

“The ad formats like pause ads, squeeze-back ads, native display ads—the foundation is there,” Prandato explained. “It’s really just building on top of that.”

Muhammad weighed in on pause ads, noting that the number of advertisers transacting with them is up dramatically this year. “Advertisers are really leaning in, and they’re finding value in terms of the returns,” he said.

articles.title: A Playbook for Marketers on Agentic Commerce
articles.fullContent:
By Justin Chin This post was created in partnership with Incubeta

As consumers integrate AI into their everyday lives, brands are looking for ways to not just be mentioned by platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini, but be recommended.

During an ADWEEK House Commerce Summit fireside chat co-hosted with Incubeta, Lauren Johnson, deputy editor of retail media and commerce at ADWEEK, sat down with Amy Crowther, CEO, Americas, at Incubeta, to discuss how AI is changing marketing and how brands can capitalize on agentic commerce.

Crowther began by sharing best practices for brands that want to be ranked prominently by AI agents. She stressed the importance of having a consistent language across every digital touchpoint, like a brand’s website, a YouTube channel, or even an FAQ page.

“It’s not the sexiest project,” Crowther said, “but it entails going in and overhauling that content, looking at where there are gaps, like an old FAQ page. AI will pick up everything that exists. And so that audit stage to begin with is really critical.”

Similarly, consistent brand storytelling and messaging across content is key. Crowther pointed out that having a large volume of content that can connect with different consumer demographics feeds the LLMs and generative AI models. She cited YouTube as an important source.

“YouTube is a big one because people forget about the advertising side of the channel,” Crowther added, sharing that some brands push their video content out on YouTube, but once they’re live on the channel, the videos become an afterthought. “

“YouTube is the predominant place that feeds the engine,” she explained. “So that’s your first place to start.”

Crowther went on to list social media sites like Instagram and Pinterest as the next areas to focus on for brand consistency when doing an AI audit.

Crowther also works with creatives and has seen the power of AI when designing campaigns. She shared an experience with a travel luggage brand that debated whether campaigns should feature just the product or include people. According to Crowther, this discussion went on for years.

“We ran the creative through our intelligence agents, and the minute a face comes onto the screen, all the focus goes off the product,” Crowther recalled. “We tied that back to the brand’s media campaigns over the last two years, and there was a downward trajectory whenever that happened. Product wins—don’t put a face in the ad.”

Crowther emphasized the value of the “feedback loop” AI creates within creative workflows, allowing marketers to adjust campaigns while they’re running. She said this changes the traditional approach to campaign planning and execution.

“If I can leave one thing with you, it’s to get away from this idea of ‘we build the plan, then we execute, and then we ask, did it work?’ I challenge that completely,” Crowther shared.

She encouraged marketers instead to “build the engine, get the momentum going, and then iterate. That has to be the new way—with media, creative data, and your own infrastructure being connected; it’s the only way to unlock incrementality.”

articles.title: Can Media Budgets Go Big on Brand Building and Still Drive Sales?
articles.fullContent:
By Dawn Papandrea This post was created in partnership with Marketing Architects

Success means planning strategies for the present and the future.

The channels and platforms brands need to understand how to navigate are constantly changing, so marketers need to adapt.

Part of navigating that landscape means crafting unique messaging for each.

There are many avenues today for capturing demand and driving sales. But sacrificing slow and steady brand building to focus just on quick wins that satisfy the CFO could set brands up for future irrelevance.

During an ADWEEK House Commerce Summit group chat co-hosted with Marketing Architects, industry leaders discussed the importance of a two-fold marketing strategy that drives both immediate revenue goals and long-lasting consumer loyalty.

Capturing demand and demonstrating the results is clean and neat in the short term, but what happens next? That key question, and theme of the session, was introduced by Clark Hjelmstad, VP of strategic partnerships at Marketing Architects.

“When that immediate demand capture starts to run dry, what do brands do?” he asked. Successful marketers, he answered, plan for both today and tomorrow. “You need to be grabbing that demand in market right now at this time, while also building for the future.”

Katie Sheeran, VP of marketing at sweetgreen, shared her strategy for making that very argument to the C-suite.

“Let’s look at the next 18 months. You show that ROAS starts to tick down and down and down,” Sheeran said. “If you’re not priming the pump and welcoming people in, those numbers are going to get a lot worse.”

Evan Jones, former CMO of Fender, likened such conversations to a dance vs. a static conversation.

“The best conversations, the best strategy, the best decisions come out of the positive tension between who we’re serving today versus who we’re trying to reach; what’s working now, what might work later,” Jones said.

Back when Sarah Davis, founder, president, and chief creative officer of FASHIONPHILE, launched the designer luxury resale company, there were no Google Ads, Pinterest, TikTok, or Instagram. But today brands must set themselves apart amid a sea of competition across various channels.

Her team’s goal for reaching the consumer who might have 100 choices in front of them is to be the brand that gets them to reach this conclusion: “Oh my gosh, there’s FASHIONPHILE. I trust them. Their ship is fast and fair. It’s going to be authentic,’” Davis explained.

Star Sage, VP of business development at Hyperice, remarked on the added challenge of trying to market a brand that started in the training rooms of pro athletes to consumers.

“Our sales team is basically brand storytellers to the audiences that we’re trying to find,” Sage shared. “Most of our consumers don’t even know that they want our product.  It’s a lot of experimenting most of the time.”

Jones elaborated that Fender has also done a lot of learning about audiences through social media marketing trial and error.

“We launched an Instagram page at one point around just new players,” Jones shared. “What we found was there are places where beginners have universal problems, so a new segment has a universal issue, but they don’t want to be isolated and kept separate from the bigger community and the bigger brand experience.”

Ultimately, Fender decided to lean into stories and brand positioning that celebrated the journey, whether you’re a professional artist or somebody who’s just getting started. “We probably failed way more than we succeeded, but at the same time, we more than tripled the business,” he said.

You can’t build a brand reputation online by simply reposting the same content everywhere, Davis attested.

“We recognize that we have to also acknowledge the platform,” she said. As an example, when FASHIONPHILE’s usual elevated voice wasn’t breaking through on TikTok Shop, they brought on creators who could talk about the brand and its offerings in a more platform-aligned way.

“We’re not changing who we are, but we’re showing up in a way that is resonating with the audience that you’re finding there,” Davis said. “The sales are evidence that this is actually working.”

To explain the delicate balance of channel planning, Sheeran used a frog metaphor. She explained that frogs have fixed skeletal structures, but also amazing elasticity.

“You have to think about: What are those bones that are absolutely non-negotiable?  What needs to show up every single place you go, everywhere you hop?” she explained. “But then also, how do you challenge yourself to be as flexible and rubbery and frog-like as possible?”

Being malleable to the platform you’re on is crucial, agreed Kristin Patterson, VP of omnichannel retail at Pinterest. That said, she pointed out, Pinterest can help brands across the funnel.

“If you are on Pinterest, you should have your full product catalog—all your feed, product—on a white background,” she said, to reach the customers who are ready to convert. But having creator assets ready can help you catch the attention of consumers open to exploring, too. “You’re letting our algorithm and the AI surface what’s best for that person in the moment to be highly personalized,” she said.

Regardless of platform, Hjelmstad said building brand credibility is key. “We’ve had a lot of success bringing brands from digital into television to gain that credibility, to stand out.”

Sarah Davis, Founder, President, and Chief Creative Officer, FASHIONPHILE

Clark Hjelmstad, VP, Strategic Partnerships, Marketing Architects

Kristin Patterson, VP, Omnichannel Retail, Pinterest

articles.title: GTA VI Shouldn’t Be Your Brand’s Only Gaming Strategy
articles.fullContent:
By Chris Erb As our industry counts down to the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI , I reflect back to a moment that shaped how I think about gaming. I was at E3 2001 and was given the opportunity to get hands-on with Grand Theft Auto III . I’d played GTA 2 on PC a couple years earlier, so I understood the franchise, but what I was seeing now was something else entirely. A true, fully realized 3D open world. A city that felt populated, alive, and full of possibility. Characters with personality. And gameplay opportunities around every corner. Rockstar’s vision was unmistakable.

At the time, I was marketing the Pokémon Trading Card Game at Wizards of the Coast, building on my previous gaming experience at GameWorks, before leaving the tabletop business to join the Madden NFL franchise at EA SPORTS, where I eventually became Vice President of Brand Marketing. My time at EA taught me something fundamental: the connections that brands build between games and their fanbases are powerful. Gamers represent a blue ocean, an enormous, engaged, and largely untapped audience for brands.

Grand Theft Auto VI will be a culturally destabilizing event, a game that will reshape the gaming market, where all cultural gravity will be focused on a single product in which all other forms of entertainment will imitate. It is expected to easily outperform the former biggest entertainment launch of all time, Avengers: Endgame , and make more than the combined box office revenue of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three .

Grand Theft Auto VI is the tip of the spear for console gaming’s resurgence. Industry data partner Circana recently reported physical video game software unit sales up 40% year-over-year, with digital marketplaces setting new concurrent user records almost every month. There are now 150 million new consoles in the market, and more games being released for them than ever before. Gaming has continued to extend its lead as the dominant global entertainment segment.

With all of this momentum we’re seeing a ton of brands dipping their toe in the gaming market right now, attempting to recreate the aesthetic of Grand Theft Auto VI , trying to be a part of the conversation. But Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t a fit for brands that are used to risk-adverse advertising campaigns. And truthfully, Rockstar doesn’t need a brand marketing partner. When the entire world is expected to buy your game on day one, there’s nothing a brand could offer that moves the needle. Brands are better off collaborating with gaming properties that are seeking support and fit their cultural ethos, joining those in the gaming space who have already figured this out.

For those looking to figure out how to authentically market to gamers, there’s already a fair number of successful case studies we’ve been a part of.

The beauty brand OPI consistently explores ways of engaging with new audiences. Women make up 50% of the video game audience but remain underserved in the market. They worked with Xbox to come up with a colorful partnership: a nail polish line aimed directly at female gamers, which saw immediate sellouts, backed by an experiential campaign in select Target stores. The program’s success led to a second activation the following year that expanded beyond beauty to include the Sunkissed Vibes OPI Special Edition Xbox Controller.

IKEA recently tackled a different segment entirely: the physical environment where gaming happens. Both brands’ top designers collaborated on a collection focused on the gamer’s space, solving problems they’re really good at: cord clutter, controller posture, and adaptable living setups. Its popularity demonstrated how a brand can find an original, authentic way to connect with gamers by genuinely improving their experience.

Fanta found a rare opening in the beverage category that fit their evolving entertainment strategy. They partnered with Xbox as an entry point to bring gamers their delicious Fanta and exclusive in-game rewards. Fanta continued their reputation of going big, and this one included promotional cans being distributed in over sixty countries. Each can was wrapped in exclusive artwork and the collaboration featured an entirely new flavor, Fanta Crimson Sour Cherry. The activation saw over a billion online impressions before a single dollar of media spend was used, a credit to the enthusiasm both fanbases have for their products.

Trolli entered the space after their data revealed that gaming was their audience’s biggest hobby. We helped them build a long-term strategy anchored by exclusive giveaways through unique CPG collaborations and League Trolli, an ongoing esports program that connected them with gamers through competition and prizes. This created an always-on consistency that formed an authentic, reliable relationship with their core demographic.

These successful activations within the gaming community require a complete understanding of the gaming experience. Brands succeed when they move beyond superficial advertising and instead deliver tangible value that resonates with gaming audiences, earning organic buzz and fan enthusiasm as a result. Finding an authentic point of connection with gamers through a brand’s existing strengths creates the inflection point of success. Brands should offer genuine value, whether that’s representation, utility, exclusivity, or sustained engagement, in a way that feels true to both the brands and gaming community.

Grand Theft Auto V shipped in 2013 and has gone on to sell 230 million copies. In the thirteen years since, we’ve watched pioneering brands enter mainstream gaming and find enormous success, while others have yet to figure out their own true path. Brands can’t be a tourist in the gaming space. Don’t let another thirteen years pass before creating a strategy for the biggest entertainment market in the world.

Chris Erb is the head of gaming at CAA Brand Consulting, a division of leading entertainment and sports agency Creative Artists Agency (CAA). Based in Los Angeles, Erb brings expertise across traditional gaming, entertainment, and culture. He oversees potential client opportunities and gaming strategies, working collaboratively across the division to ensure the best teams and expertise are brought forward. Erb has worked with gaming clients, including Microsoft, Bethesda, CD Projekt Red, and Sega, as well as traditional brands, including WK Kellogg’s, Doritos, and Fanta. Prior to CAA Brand Consulting, Erb worked at Electronic Arts, where he led its Madden NFL franchise and EA SPORTS brand.

articles.title: 5 Questions For …MS NOW Executive Producers On One Year Anniversary Of Name Change
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro On November 15, 2025, Versant switched the name of its news network from MSNBC to MS NOW. The new name, which stands for My Source for News, Opinion and the World, had to build alot of its infrastructure from scratch after detaching from NBC News.

The switch to a new name did not affect viewership, as the network ranked second among all cable networks in total viewers during the third quarter. In addition, in the past year it launched its direct-to-consumer platform, MS NOW Membership.

Some of the people who have witnessed all these changes up close are the executive producers of MS NOW’s linear shows. They have been responsible for establishing the new name in their programs as well as ensuring the mission remains the same even after the transition.

In recognition of MS NOW’s first anniversary, TVNewser spoke to five executive producers, who launched new shows within the first year. They Include, State of Play with Peter Alexander ’s Sandi Cohen , On the Line with Alicia Menendez ’s Marti Hause , The 11th Hour with Ali Velshi ’s Rebekah Dryden , Connect with Jacob Soboroff ’s Dina Moss , and Joy Fowlin from The Assignment with Antonia Hylton .

(This interview has been edited for length)

TVNewser: How has the first year known as MS NOW been?

Cohen : I’ve only been here for the last six months, but the energy is unmatched. There’s a feeling of positivity and building towards the future, and a real team effort to do so. It’s been inspiring and given me a boost.

Hause : It has been a really exciting year at MS NOW. It’s been remarkable to see this entire organization build from the ground up, driving toward the ultimate goal of serving our viewers.

Dryden: I think of the first year as MS NOW as a year of proving it, a series of rapid-fire, real-time proof points of who we are and what we can do as a network, standing up on our own.

Moss : When MS NOW first relaunched, I never would have imagined we’d be here. It’s been the greatest honor and challenge to launch Connect alongside Jacob and our team.

Fowlin : Two words to describe the first year as MS NOW: seamless and exciting. Change can be hard, but everyone worked together to make the transition as smooth as possible. It was truly a testament of leading from the top.

TN: What does the new network name signify for you and your program?

Cohen : We’re meeting the moment! “NOW” is right in the name. A constant reminder of why we do what we do, and to meet that mission.

Hause : The new name signifies to me that we are covering the day’s news with hosts, reporters and guests who bring a depth of expertise and experience to help our viewers navigate the stakes of what we are seeing.

Dryden : “News, Opinion, World” has always been our work. But I especially love what “My Source” says about who we’ve become. By 11 o’clock, people have had the whole day’s news thrown at them. Being someone’s source means answering that with facts they can trust, and then sending them to bed with something to hold onto.

Moss : We hope that our audience sees us as their ‘source’ for connection and community. What we’ve really been prioritizing on Connect are voices and stories that our viewers can relate to.

Fowlin : MS NOW stands for accuracy, precision, and collaboration. I am so proud to work with a team and an entire network of people who truly enjoy coming to work every day.

TN: As the leaders of new programs on MS NOW, how has it gone so far?

Cohen : We’re having a blast. Nearly every day Peter tells me how fun doing this show is. And he’s right. We have a wonderful team of smart and kind producers who work incredibly hard.

Hause : It has been such an invigorating process. Starting a new show has been a total reset on how we cover the news of the day. For On The Line, it’s a constant discussion about how we focus on the stakes of any given story, not the odds. Dryden : It has been a joy to lead a new chapter of The 11th Hour with Ali Velshi. We both feel so privileged to have been given the opportunity to take up the 11th Hour mantle and trusted with the freedom to make it our own.

Moss : Long nights, early mornings, and a ton of coffee! But the most fun I’ve had in my career.

Fowlin : Launching The Assignment has been one of the best opportunities of my career. I had never built a show from scratch, and what a privilege it was to do. I inherited an incredible team of producers who embraced the show’s vision.

TN: What similarities have you seen between relaunching MS NOW and starting a new program?

Cohen : Our show has had to find our voice, our people, and our mission. It takes a lot of trial and error. Leaders across the company are doing the same thing. Whether that’s for our digital products, in-person experiences, or linear TV.

Hause : I see a lot of similarities in the way we’ve questioned conventional wisdom and our processes. It’s led to some great changes to the status quo and brought new opportunities for members of our team.

Dryden : Cable news producers have always been a scrappy and industrious group, and there was a real sense of building something together as we launched this new show and this new network. So every challenge felt like a team effort and, in the end, an accomplishment.

Moss : What I’ve enjoyed so much is the collaboration. When we relaunched MS NOW, there was collective effort to make it a success. I feel the same about launching Connect with Jacob Soboroff. It’s been a melding of minds (and some of the brightest minds in the industry, at that).

Fowlin : Yes, putting together a new show does require a start-up mentality. You need grit, drive, flexibility, and a good dose of fearlessness. We all come together with the same mission: to put together a news program centered on the human stories behind the headlines.

TN: What’s one interesting nugget you can share about your anchor?

Cohen : Peter Alexander does not drink coffee. Even when we’re traveling and working long days, there is no caffeine, and he really doesn’t need it.

articles.title: How the TikTok algorithm works in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. The TikTok algorithm recommends content based on three signal types: user interactions, video information, and account settings, with watch time and completion rate carrying the most weight.
  2. Hooking viewers in the first 3 seconds is critical, because early watch time is the strongest ranking signal.
  3. TikTok SEO matters as much as hashtags now. The algorithm analyzes captions, voiceovers, and on-screen text to categorize your content and surface it in search.
  4. Consistent posting, community alignment, and tracking analytics are what separate sustained growth from one-off viral moments.

What is the TikTok algorithm in 2026?

The TikTok algorithm is the technology that decides what TikTok videos to recommend to each user. It studies what you watch and how you interact, and then suggests videos you’re most likely to enjoy.

No two TikTok users will see the same combination of TikTok videos on their For You Page. This feed is unique and highly personalized. The type of content you see on your FYP will evolve over time, as the algorithm catches on to changes in your interests and viewing preferences.

According to TikTok’s official documentation: “We use recommender systems to offer you a personalized experience. These systems suggest content based on your preferences as expressed through interactions on TikTok, such as following an account or liking a post.”

In short: the For You feed is a personalized recommendation engine, and your job as a marketer is to give it clear signals about who your content is for.

Bonus: Get a free TikTok Growth Checklist from famous TikTok creator Tiffy Chen that shows you how to gain 1.6 million followers with only 3 studio lights and iMovie.

How does the TikTok algorithm work in 2026?

The TikTok algorithm looks at three main signals when ranking content. Of these, engagement signals like watch time and completion rate carry the most weight, and TikTok continuously refines how it weighs the rest.

  1. User interactions: What you watch, like, share, comment on, or skip.
  2. Video information: Captions, hashtags, sounds, effects, and views.
  3. User information: Language, country, device type, and settings.

1. User interactions

Every action you take on TikTok provides the app with information about what kind of content you’re most interested in. Within this category, watch time and completion rate are the strongest signals. If someone watches your video all the way through, or replays it, that tells the algorithm your content is highly engaging.

Here are some of the user interactions that will impact what shows up on your For You feed:

  • Videos you’ve liked or shared on the app
  • Videos you’ve added to your favorites
  • Videos you’ve marked as “Not Interested”
  • Videos you’ve reported as inappropriate
  • Interests you’ve expressed by interacting with organic content and ads
  • Which accounts you follow
  • Comments you’ve posted
  • Creators or sounds you’ve chosen to hide
  • How long you spend watching a video (and whether you replay it)
  • Content you create on your own account

Positive signals tell the algorithm to show you more of the same kind of content, while the negative ones will prevent similar content from showing up in your feed.

2. Video information

The TikTok algorithm also collects information about the videos you look for in search and the types of videos you watch in general.

Video information signals include:

  • Captions
  • Sounds
  • Hashtags
  • Effects
  • Trending topics
  • Video length

It’s worth noting that TikTok doesn’t just read your metadata. The algorithm can also analyze on-screen text and spoken words to understand what your video is about. This means your voiceover and text overlays are categorization signals too, not just your caption and hashtags.

3. User information

User information doesn’t have as much influence as user actions or video details, but they still play a role. Some of the user information triggers included in the TikTok algorithm are:

  • Language preference
  • Country setting (you may be more likely to see content from people in your own country, or videos that are particularly popular in your country)
  • Device type
  • Categories of interest you selected in your new user preferences
  • Time zone and day

These are the settings that help TikTok run smoothly. But, because they’re based on one-time settings, rather than ongoing activity, they aren’t as important to the algorithm.

Does TikTok use a point system?

You may have seen claims that TikTok assigns specific point values to each type of interaction, like 1 point for a like and 5 points for a share. TikTok has not publicly confirmed any such point system.

What we do know is that TikTok uses weighted signals, meaning some interactions matter more than others. Based on TikTok’s documentation and observed behavior, here’s how those signals generally stack up:

  • Strongest signals: Watch time, completion rate, replays, shares
  • Strong signals: Comments, follows from the video, saves/favorites
  • Moderate signals: Likes, hashtag engagement
  • Weaker signals: Device type, language, location

  1. Short-form video defined: Video content typically under 60 seconds, built for vertical, mobile-first platforms like TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Snapchat Spotlight.
  2. Why it matters for marketing: Most consumers prefer short video when learning about a product, and platform algorithms surface it to people who do not already follow you.

What is short-form video?

Short-form video is video content typically under 60 seconds, created for vertical, mobile-first platforms. Short videos are intended to be quick, easily digestible content for viewers scrolling through social media feeds or other outlets.

The definition has shifted as platforms raised their limits. TikTok now accepts uploads far longer than a minute, and YouTube Shorts allows up to three minutes. But the practical sweet spot has not moved much: the videos that get watched all the way through are still short.

Common examples of short-form videos include TikTok videos, Instagram Stories and Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Snapchat Spotlight and Stories.

Short-form vs. long-form video

Long-form video usually runs longer than two minutes and is built for depth: tutorials, interviews, documentaries, product walkthroughs. Short-form video is built for attention: it earns a view from someone who was not looking for you.

Here is how the two formats compare.

Most strategies benefit from both. Short-form video is where you win attention, and long-form is where you keep it.

Why does short-form video matter for marketing in 2026?

Short-form video matters because it is how most people now prefer to learn about products, and because platforms distribute it to audiences you have not built yet.

Short-form video content isn’t new. In fact, Vine, the short-form video app that launched publicly in January 2013, was an early pioneer of the format. But what started as a niche platform has grown into something much larger, with Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube all building short-form video features of their own.

Consumer preference is the clearest signal. Data from Wyzowl found that short videos seem to perform best when marketers assess video ROI, and that, given the choice, most people would prefer to learn about a product through a short explainer video versus other content.

Reach follows the same pattern. On YouTube, Shorts average more than 200 billion daily views, which gives even small channels a realistic shot at discovery.

Part of the appeal is practical. With an average video length of 15 to 30 seconds, creators can deliver their message in a very small window of time, allowing viewers to consume content on the go with little to no commitment.

Short-form videos can also be shared and watched from any device, which furthers their accessibility and popularity among users. From sending Snapchat stories on the subway to watching YouTube Shorts in the dentist waiting room, viewers can access and engage with content at any time.

Cost is the other factor. Short-form video is generally cheap and easy to produce and requires minimal production effort. All you need is a smartphone and a good idea. Plus, hosting platforms like TikTok and Instagram are all free to use.

In short, short-form video content matters for marketers because:

  • Distribution: Algorithms surface it to non-followers, so reach is not capped by follower count
  • Cost: Production costs stay low relative to the reach it can generate
  • Consumer preference: 62% of U.S. adults prefer short-form video over text or long-form alternatives when consuming content
  • Speed: Teams can react to trends and cultural moments within hours, not weeks
  • Commerce: Shoppable formats shorten the path from view to purchase

Best platforms for short-form video in 2026

The four platforms that matter most for short-form video are TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Snapchat Spotlight. Each has a different maximum length, a different ideal length, and a different audience, so the same video rarely performs identically across all four.

Key Takeaways

  • The choice between generative engine optimization (GEO) and search engine optimization (SEO) isn’t either-or. The two disciplines complement each other.
  • SEO earns rankings in traditional search results. GEO builds the depth and authority that earn your content citations in AI-generated answers across platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews.
  • Answer engine optimization (AEO) and large language model optimization (LLMO) round out the picture. 
  • AEO helps structure your content to become the direct answer in AI-powered search experiences, from featured snippets to AI Overviews and tools like ChatGPT. LLMO shapes how large language models (LLMs) understand and describe your brand.
  • Google considers AI optimization “still SEO” because “optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience.”
  • To build a combined strategy, start with your SEO foundation. From there, structure pages for AEO and deepen content for GEO. Consistent brand information across the web supports LLMO.

If you’ve been doing SEO for a while, you’ve probably noticed a shift. SEO is no longer the only factor to consider in search visibility. 

According to Ahrefs research, Google’s AI Overviews are associated with a 58 percent lower click-through rate for top-ranking pages.

AI-powered search is reaching a massive audience. Google reports that AI Overviews has more than 2.5 billion monthly users, while AI Mode has already passed 1 billion monthly users.

At the same time, people are skipping Google altogether and using tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini for answers and recommendations. 

That’s created a wave of new terminology: GEO, SEO, AEO, LLMO, and so on. Keeping it up with it all can feel overwhelming.

Each covers a different search surface that SEO wasn’t built for. They don’t replace SEO, but you also can’t rely on SEO alone.

I get questions all the time about how SEO, GEO, AEO, and LLMO relate to one another and when each one matters. If you’re asking those same questions, this guide is for you. We’ll start with GEO vs. SEO as the foundation, then layer AEO and LLMO on top.

Defining the Four Disciplines

SEO, GEO, AEO, and LLMO each target a different surface:

  • Search engine optimization is the process of improving your site so it ranks higher in search results. It relies on content quality and site structure, backed by strong backlinks and solid technical performance, to earn visibility in Google and other engines. 
  • Generative engine optimization focuses on getting AI tools to cite or recommend your content in their answers. Those include Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. GEO emphasizes depth and expertise because generative systems prioritize trustworthy, well-supported content. Fresh, up-to-date information also carries more weight in these systems. 
  • Answer engine optimization helps your site appear as a direct answer in search results. That covers featured snippets, People Also Ask boxes, knowledge panels, voice assistant responses, and AI-generated answers in tools like ChatGPT and Google’s AI Overviews. AEO relies on clear, structured content, like FAQs and schema markup. It’s ideal for high-intent, question-based queries.
  • Large language model optimization shapes how AI models understand and describe your brand. LLMO is built on clear entities and original insights paired with a consistent brand presence across platforms.

GEO vs. SEO vs. AEO vs. LLMO: Side-by-Side Comparison

Each discipline works differently and measures success differently. Here’s how they compare side by side.

GEO vs. SEO: What Changes When AI Enters the Picture

GEO and SEO share the same mission of getting useful, credible content in front of the right audience. The mechanics differ, but the fundamentals overlap.

Here’s where they connect:

  • Both are built around user intent. You win by matching the question behind the query, not by chasing vague head terms.
  • Content quality drives outcomes. Original research and current stats increase usefulness, especially when paired with step-by-step guidance readers can act on. Covering a topic in depth is how you build topical authority.
  • Structure increases visibility. Descriptive headers and short paragraphs help crawlers and AI models process your content. Ordered lists and clear tables are especially useful for queries where users need to compare options or follow steps.

articles.title: Brand Trust: What is it and why it matters

A great product or clever marketing campaign might get someone interested in your business. But what convinces them to buy, recommend it to a friend or come back for more? It comes down to brand trust.

Consumers are getting more particular about where they place that trust. With AI-generated content raising new questions about what’s real, many are looking closer at product claims and seeking honest opinions from other customers. According to Sprout Social’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, 57% of consumers trust everyday product users most for recommendations, far ahead of subject matter experts (26%), mega-influencers (9%) and brand employees (8%).

This shift gives brands a chance to rethink how they earn consumer confidence. People want to know a business will deliver on its promises, and their experiences with a brand often speak louder than any marketing campaign. For brands that get it right, the payoff extends well beyond the initial sale.

Brand trust develops over time, shaped by everything from how a company communicates to how it handles customer concerns. Understanding what earns trust is essential to building lasting relationships.

Read on to learn what brand trust means today, why it matters for business growth and how to build, measure and maintain it.

What is brand trust?

Brand trust is consumers’ confidence in a business and its ability to meet their expectations. Several factors shape that confidence, including:

  • Your brand values and mission
  • The quality of your products or services
  • Transparency around business practices and supply chains (e.g., AI disclaimers, certifications, eco-friendly, etc.)
  • The honesty of your advertising claims (e.g., health claims, product longevity, research efficacy)
  • Your treatment of employees and manufacturers
  • An authentic brand voice that reflects your business’s values
  • Responsible, brand-safe influencer partnerships
  • Reliable customer service and care

Building trust means consistently following through on these commitments. Customers notice when a brand’s actions match its messaging, and when there’s a disconnect.

Authenticity plays an important role here. According to Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey, authenticity is the number one trait consumers value in brands on social media. That desire for authenticity extends beyond social media. Consumers want to see the same honesty reflected in how a business operates and treats its customers.

Your reputation also matters to future buyers, too. A strong track record can give potential customers the confidence to choose your brand, even if they’re unfamiliar with your products or services.

Why is building brand trust important for a strong brand?

Brand trust is more than a “feel-good” goal. It’s a concrete way to drive profitability and expansion. While no brand can maintain a perfect reputation all the time, those that earn consumers’ trust over the long term are better positioned to compete and succeed in their industry.

Enhanced loyalty and retention

When consumers trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products over competitors. Positive experiences reinforce that confidence, helping improve customer retention and reduce churn.

Product quality plays a major role in maintaining trust and loyalty. According to Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey, 44% of consumers say product or service quality is their top driver of brand loyalty. Consistently meeting customer expectations gives them a reason to stick around, even when other options are available.

Customer advocacy and evangelism

Trustworthy brands benefit from higher levels of customer advocacy, leading to valuable word-of-mouth recommendations and a stronger brand reputation. Brand trust can differentiate your brand from competitors, attract new customers, and create opportunities for future partnerships and collaborations.

This advocacy isn’t limited to customers; it can be even more impactful when it comes from key opinion leaders and thought leaders whose expert endorsements can strengthen a brand’s reputation.

Increased customer lifetime value

When consumers trust brands, they’re more likely to keep engaging over time, make repeat purchases, and upgrade to higher-value products or services. Consumers who trust a brand are also more likely to recognize the value of its products and services, making them more willing to pay a premium for the quality and experience they expect.

Building brand trust should be a key part of your wider customer retention strategy. Nurturing relationships over time can increase customer lifetime value and support more sustainable business growth.

How to build brand trust

While understanding what brand trust means is relatively straightforward, building it is much more complex. It requires a coordinated effort across your business, from internal operations to how you communicate with customers. Every department plays a role in earning and maintaining consumer confidence.

Maintain a consistent brand voice across communication channels

Consistent brand messaging helps customers recognize your business and know what to expect. Whether someone encounters your brand through an ad, visits your website or receives a marketing email, the underlying message should feel familiar.

Establish clear brand guidelines that define your tone of voice, visual identity and core messaging. These guidelines help teams stay consistent across campaigns and channels while adapting their approach to different audiences and formats.

For example, tinned seafood brand Fishwife maintains a recognizable visual identity across its website and Instagram. Its colorful packaging, playful illustrations and bold typography appear across channels, while its conversational, humorous copy gives the brand a consistent personality. Even when promoting individual products, Fishwife maintains the same distinctive look and feel that customers associate with its brand.

Your brand doesn’t need to sound exactly the same everywhere. A playful Instagram caption might feel out of place in a customer service email, for example. What matters is that customers can recognize the same brand behind both interactions.

articles.title: AI Sentiment and Accuracy: The Metric Your Visibility Dashboard Is Missing (and How to Calibrate for It)

Key Takeaways

  • Visibility and accuracy fail independently. An engine can cite you in nearly every answer and still describe you with outdated facts.
  • Score three axes, not one verdict. Rate each brand-relevant answer on accuracy, sentiment, and currency. Each axis points to a different fix.
  • Answers drift for documented reasons. Engines surface the most repeated claim. Source content that passed through unsupervised AI editing can arrive already degraded.
  • No platform offers an edit button. ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity accept feedback. None commits to changing a specific answer.
  • Source correction carries the most weight. Fixing the pages an engine cites changes the answer more reliably than any in-product report.

Every AI visibility report answers one question: are you showing up, and how often? Rank tracking, citation counts, and visibility measured at scale all count appearances. None of them tell you what the answer said about you. That blind spot is where AI sentiment and accuracy live.

Your brand can hold a strong citation rate across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity while the answer describes a product you sunset two years ago. The same answer might credit a competitor with your flagship feature, or lead with a complaint from a single review site. Your dashboard still shows green.

Visibility tells you whether you are in the conversation. Sentiment and accuracy tell you whether that helps you or hurts you. This post covers how to score both, why answers go stale, and which correction levers do real work.

Visibility Tells You If You’re in the Room. It Doesn’t Tell You What Was Said.

Citation frequency, inclusion rate, and share of voice all measure presence. An engine can name you in nine of 10 answers and still get your pricing model wrong in all nine. AI brand misrepresentation sits outside what any visibility metric detects.

Four situations call for different work.

High visibility, accurate answers. You are in good shape. Keep monitoring, because engines refresh their sources constantly.

High visibility, inaccurate answers. Your worst case, and the one a dashboard hides. The engine repeats you often and repeats you wrong, so every citation amplifies the error.

Low visibility, accurate answers. A reach problem. You need more citable, authoritative coverage. NP Digital’s study of 9 million AI answers found that owned citations deliver the single strongest visibility lift in the data.

Low visibility, inaccurate answers. Two jobs at once. Fix the source material first, then push for citations, or you will scale the wrong story.

In the past, this site has covered how AI answers compress a brand’s first impression, and how defending your brand in AI results starts with governance. That piece explains the problem. This one gives you the scoring system, because you cannot govern what you have not measured.

A quarterly report with rising citation counts can cover a quarter in which your reputation got worse. The numbers improve while the answers degrade, and nothing in the report connects the two.

Why AI Answers Drift Out of Date and Out of Alignment

Two documented mechanisms explain most of what an audit turns up. Neither one is a conspiracy against your brand. Both are structural.

Engines Weight Repetition, Not Verification

Language models surface the claim that appears most consistently across their sources. A hundred directory pages carrying your 2021 address outweigh one corrected About page, and the engine cannot tell which version is true. Confident phrasing says nothing about input quality. The Tow Center for Digital Journalism tested eight AI search tools and found that they answered more than 60 percent of queries incorrectly. Perplexity performed best, and still got 37 percent wrong. Every wrong answer arrived in the same assured tone as a right one. Our own NP Digital has shown that nearly half of marketers deal with AI errors multiple times a week.

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Cross-posting defined: Sharing adapted versions of the same content across multiple social platforms to save time and extend reach.
  2. Why identical posts backfire: Publishing the exact same copy and creative everywhere can read as spam to your audience and perform poorly against platform algorithms.
  3. What good cross-posting looks like: Tailoring captions, visuals, hashtags, and formatting to each platform’s specs and audience before you publish.
  4. How to do it at scale: Tools like Hootsuite Social OS let you customize, schedule, and measure cross-posted content from one workspace.

What is cross-posting on social media?

Cross-posting is the process of posting similar content across multiple social media channels. Social media managers use the tactic to help save time and resources. No more crafting a unique social media update for each channel every time you need to post.

The key word is similar, not identical. Cross-posting works when you start from one core message and then adapt it for each platform’s format, character limits, and audience.

It has also become harder to avoid, with social media platforms now reaching an estimated 5.75 billion users. Most brands now maintain a presence on five or more networks, and with people spending an average of two hours and 21 minutes a day on social media, there is real upside to getting your message in front of audiences wherever they spend their time.

Alongside saving time, cross-posting is a highly effective tactic for social managers because it helps streamline their posting strategy, allows them to repurpose content across multiple platforms, and continually keeps their social channels up to date. It is also easier to execute well than it used to be, since AI-assisted social media management tools can now draft platform-specific variations of a single post in seconds.

Who is cross-posting good for?

  • Enterprise and mid-market social teams managing multi-brand, multi-region, or franchise accounts, where one campaign message needs to land consistently across dozens of profiles
  • Agency social media managers running publishing calendars for several clients at once
  • Companies with smaller budgets
  • Startups and founders who are running social alongside doing everything else
  • New brands that haven’t developed a lot of content yet
  • Time-conscious creators who want to free up hours to spend on delivering engaging, compelling posts

Cross-posting vs. content repurposing

Cross-posting and content repurposing get used interchangeably, but they are different jobs. Cross-posting takes one message and adapts it for multiple platforms, keeping the format mostly intact. Repurposing transforms content into an entirely new format for a new purpose.

A product launch graphic posted to Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn with tailored captions is cross-posting. Turning a webinar recording into six short vertical clips, a carousel, and a blog recap is repurposing.

Use cross-posting when the message is self-contained and travels well. Use repurposing when the original asset is too long, too dense, or wrong for the format you are targeting. Most strong content calendars use both.

What are the benefits of cross-posting?

The main benefit of cross-posting on social media is output: more presence across more channels without multiplying your production workload. A few more worth planning around:

  • Time savings: One brief, one creative asset, and a handful of caption edits replaces building each post from scratch.
  • Wider reach across different audiences: Platform demographics barely overlap. The same announcement can reach a LinkedIn audience in their 30s and 40s and an Instagram audience under 30, where 80% of adults 18 to 29 are active.
  • More consistent brand messaging: Starting from a single core message keeps campaign language aligned across channels, which matters most when several people publish on behalf of the brand.
  • Better use of your best content: Your top-performing posts deserve more than one shot at an audience.
  • Cleaner performance comparisons: Running the same message across platforms shows you where a given asset actually resonates, which sharpens future planning.
  • Always-on channels: Quieter platforms stay active instead of going dormant between dedicated campaigns.

What are the risks of cross-posting?

Cross-posting goes wrong when adaptation gets skipped. These are the failure points to watch:

  • Content fatigue: Followers who find you on three platforms and see the same post three times have a reason to unfollow two of them.
  • Weaker algorithmic performance: Platforms reward native formats. Reposted videos carrying another app’s watermark or logo tend to get less distribution.
  • Tone mismatches: Copy written for X often reads as flippant on LinkedIn, and LinkedIn copy reads as stiff on TikTok.
  • Broken mechanics: Dead handle tags, clickable links that are not clickable, cropped images, and truncated captions all signal carelessness.
  • Narrower discoverability: Reusing one hashtag set everywhere ignores how differently each platform surfaces and ranks tagged content.

  1. Reddit marketing works best when brands participate authentically in niche communities instead of pushing promotional content.
  2. With more than 100,000 active subreddits and an audience that often isn’t reachable elsewhere (40% of Redditors aren’t on TikTok), Reddit gives brands access to communities they can’t find on other platforms.

What is Reddit marketing?

Reddit marketing is the practice of using Reddit to reach an audience, either by participating organically in subreddit discussions or by running paid Reddit ads. Unlike feed-based platforms, Reddit is forum-driven and built around niche communities called subreddits, so success depends on how well you fit the culture of a specific community rather than how often you post.

And Redditors? They’re famously opinionated.

As a Redditor myself, that’s part of the charm. Reddit is humor-driven, deeply specific, and filled with real, down-to-earth people who definitely don’t respond well to obvious marketing.

But for brands that understand the culture, Reddit can be one of the most powerful platforms for building trust, credibility, and brand awareness.

For other organizations that are a bit more serious, like central banks or the World Health Organization, Reddit is probably not the top choice as a digital marketing channel.

What kind of brands succeed on Reddit?

Brands succeed on Reddit when their approach matches how the platform works. Reddit is built around conversation, so the brands that do well tend to be the ones that listen first and talk second. Reddit tends to work best for brands that:

  • Can provide genuine value (insight, expertise, transparency)

  • Thread: A chain of replies under a Reddit post.

Think of social media guidelines as your brand’s manual for social media best practices. They should outline how to behave on social media in a way that’s positive and safe.

The forms on your website are full of opportunity. Unfortunately, not everyone gets forms right, and they don’t convert the way they should. 

Simply putting a form on a landing page doesn’t guarantee people will submit. 

One study showed that more than half of people who visit a form fail to successfully complete it. Since forms are a gateway to lead generation, that’s a lot of missed opportunity. 

Why aren’t people clicking or completing?

If you don’t optimize your forms for users, they’re more likely to abandon them or not even click into them at all.

So, how do you increase form conversions?

A few tweaks like form placement, field count, color, and copy can turn your forms into a key driver of lead generation, which is exactly what this article will cover. Read on to start generating the leads you need to scale and grow. 

1. Place the Form Where It Gets Seen

Form placement dictates how many visitors see your form. Attention still clusters at the top of the page, where users spend more time. That said, placement should shift based on factors like user intent and what you’re asking visitors to commit to. 

Industry plays a role, too. B2B brands, for example, typically see higher average time spent on page than retail brands.

Why?

Higher-intent users, like those shopping for a specific product at a store, tend to convert better on shorter pages. They know what they want (and they want it fast). A call-to-action (CTA) or form makes sense at the very top of the page, or even as a pop-up.  

Gap.com, for instance, uses a pop-up to capture user attention with a 15 percent-off discount.

Saving money doesn’t need much explanation, so it makes sense to put this front and center.

Lower-intent users want more information before making a decision, especially for complex products or services, such as booking a software demo. They need to understand what you do and why it matters to them. 

Deel pulls this off well. It offers enterprise cybersecurity tools and wants users to book a demo to learn more. This page asks a few questions about what the user wants before the link to book. 

Users get a clear view of what Deel does and can consider their services before booking a demo. 

Device type also matters because the fold moves by device. According to StatCounter, the most common desktop resolution is 1920×1080 (28.1 percent). Top mobile screen resolutions include 414×896 (13.3 percent) and 360×800 (7.6 percent).

A smaller device like a phone could push the form down below other elements like the header or hero image, and users may never even see it.

2. Ensure You Have a Strong Call-to-Action

The call-to-action is the tipping point between conversions and bounce. It drives action and conversions, which is what you want.

Not all CTAs do the job well, however. Something as simple as a word or color can affect conversion rates.  

For example, a button that says “Submit” asks for effort without a clear value proposition.
